metadata.title: Measurements of skill and skill-use using PIAAC

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PIAAC microdata covering 24 countries (PIAAC Round 1: 2008–2013; Round 2: 2012–2016) and constructs literacy and numeracy skill and skill-use indices using IRT-based models. The authors restrict the analytic sample to prime-age adults (25–59), exclude full-time students and permanently disabled individuals, exclude the problem-solving module, and drop observations with missing values in variables needed for analysis (item non-response is described as limited at 3.3%). The paper does not report the use of PIAAC complex survey weights or any specific weight variable (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT), and it also does not describe replicate-weight variance estimation. Because the analysis is primarily based on IRT estimation and subsequent regression/censored Tobit/Heckit-style models rather than ML training, the manuscript provides no explicit weighting strategy for population-representative inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not use PIAAC-provided plausible values (PV) as dependent variables; instead, it constructs its own literacy and numeracy skill scores and skill-use indices using IRT (two-parameter logistic for skills; general partial credit model for ordered skill-use frequencies). Because the dependent variables are IRT-derived latent traits/indices rather than PV-based achievement scores, PV handling is not applicable. For missing data, the authors state that they exclude observations with missing values in variables necessary for analysis and note that item non-response is relatively rare, but they do not explicitly classify the missing-data procedure using a standard PV/missing-data framework (e.g., listwise deletion vs imputation), so the missing-data handling is treated as not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses PIAAC Round 1 (2008–2013) and Round 2 (2012–2016) participating countries, but excludes Australia and Indonesia because their datasets are not provided for public use, and excludes Russia’s dataset for Moscow residents. The authors further exclude 6 countries because they lack some social-institution indices used in Section 3.2, leaving a main analysis sample of 24 countries. They restrict the sample to prime-age adults aged 25–59 at the time of the survey, exclude full-time students and permanently disabled individuals, exclude the problem-solving section (only literacy and numeracy are used), and exclude observations with missing values in variables necessary for the analysis. They also note that item non-response is relatively rare and that the fraction dropped due to missing values is limited to 3.3%.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC Round 1 (2008–2013) & Round 2 (2012–2016) — literacy skill and literacy skill use (prime-age 25–59; problem-solving excluded)
main_findings.target_variable: Immigrant-native wage penalty explained by gaps in literacy skill and literacy skill use (Gelbach decomposition)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Text reports: immigrant wage penalty in 16 of 20 countries; in 6 countries (Estonia, Germany, Italy, Korea, Slovenia, Spain) the penalty is substantially reduced after controlling for covariates including skill and skill use. Gelbach decomposition (Figure 9): in these 6 countries, the contribution of literacy use to the explained immigrant-native wage gap is 25–36%, while the contribution of literacy skill varies (less than 10% in Italy and Spain; about 25% in Estonia and Germany). Additional analysis (Gender wage gap explained by gender gaps in literacy skill and literacy skill use): Figure 7 reports country-level unadjusted vs adjusted gender wage gaps and Gelbach (2016) decomposition. In Japan, the unadjusted gap is 45% and shrinks to 24% after conditioning on demographics, skill, and skill use; in Korea, 26% shrinks to 14%. Decomposition indicates that about 50% of the explained gender gap in Japan and Korea is attributable to tenure and about 25% to literacy use; in Belgium and the UK, literacy use contributes around 60% of the explained gap; in Norway, almost all of the explained gap is attributed to literacy use. Additional analysis (Hourly wage (log) — association with literacy skill and literacy skill use): Regression estimates (Table 2): one-standard-deviation increases in literacy skill and literacy skill use are associated with 6.0% and 9.8% increases in hourly wages (Column 1). After controlling for occupation dummies, the associations attenuate to 4.8% (skill) and 6.6% (skill-use) (Column 2). Standard errors clustered by country and skill quartile group; N=12,790; Countries=21.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC Round 1 and Round 2 the study leveraged immigrant status together with literacy skill and literacy skill use to explain the immigrant-native wage penalty, finding that in countries where the penalty is reduced after adjustment, a non-negligible share of the explained gap is attributable to differences in literacy utilization (25–36%). This indicates that skill mismatch operates through underutilization of skills on the job, suggesting immigration and labor-market integration policies should focus on matching immigrants to roles that enable effective skill use, not only on credential recognition.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC Round 1 (2008–2013) & Round 2 (2012–2016) — literacy skill use (prime-age 25–59; problem-solving excluded)
main_findings.target_variable: Literacy skill use — effect of parental leave on the gender gap in skill use (censored Tobit; extensive + intensive margins)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 (censored Tobit; full sample including non-working): coefficients for Female × PL × Literacy skill quartile. For Q3, one-year-longer paid parental leave widens the gender gap in literacy use by 0.24 SD (reported in text; Table 3 shows negative coefficients for higher quartiles, with Q3: -0.238*** in Column 1; Q2: -0.173***; Q4: -0.109*). Adding institutional controls (Columns 2–4) does not significantly change impacts; coefficients for Q2 and Q3 range between -0.16 and -0.20 and -0.25 and -0.30, respectively. Intensive-margin OLS among employed (Column 5): Q2 and Q3 remain statistically significant with about two-thirds and one-third of the full-sample estimates. Observations: 48,970; Countries: 24.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC Round 1 and Round 2 the study leveraged parental leave duration and gender (interacted with literacy-skill quartiles) to predict literacy skill use, finding that longer paid parental leave widens the gender gap in literacy use among modestly skilled women (e.g., Q3: about 0.24 SD per additional year) and that the effect persists at the intensive margin among employed workers. This indicates that expanding parental-leave policies can entail a trade-off: it may support labor-force participation for lower-skilled women while simultaneously reducing intensive skill utilization for moderately skilled women, informing policy design to mitigate role- and hours-based underutilization.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC Round 1 (2008–2013) & Round 2 (2012–2016) — wage gap by years since immigration (with literacy skill and literacy skill use controls)
main_findings.target_variable: Wage gap between immigrants and natives over years since immigration (and its decomposition)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Figure 10/text: raw wage gap is 19% for 0–4 years since immigration and 22% for 5–9 years, then narrows and becomes close to 0 after 25–29 years. After adjusting for age, gender, education, tenure, literacy skill, and literacy use (country-specific coefficients), these covariates explain more than one half of the raw wage gap in the 0–9 years since immigration, and the difference between raw and adjusted gaps gradually becomes small. Decomposition indicates that differences in tenure, literacy skill, and literacy use explain the persistent wage gap, and the gap explained by literacy use narrows as years since immigration increases.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC Round 1 and Round 2 the study leveraged immigrant status and controls including literacy skill and literacy skill use to model how the immigrant-native wage gap evolves with years since immigration, finding that the wage gap narrows toward zero after 25–29 years and that the portion explained by literacy-use differences diminishes over time. This indicates that assimilation into jobs that better utilize skills can be a key mechanism behind wage convergence, implying that labor-market policies supporting language acquisition and occupational matching may accelerate effective skill utilization.

data.outcome_summary: This paper constructs new, internationally comparable measures of literacy and numeracy skill and skill use using OECD PIAAC microdata from 24 countries (PIAAC Round 1: 2008–2013; Round 2: 2012–2016), restricting to prime-age adults (25–59), excluding the problem-solving module, and excluding observations with missing values in analysis variables. The authors do not use PIAAC-provided plausible values; instead, they estimate latent traits via IRT (two-parameter logistic for skills; general partial credit model for ordered skill-use frequencies) and normalize indices. Across applications, the study shows that skill use is strongly associated with wages within occupations (e.g., 9.8% vs 6.0% wage increases for one SD higher literacy use vs literacy skill, attenuating to 6.6% vs 4.8% after occupation controls). It further finds that parental leave length widens the gender gap in literacy use among modestly skilled women (with effects persisting at the intensive margin), and that immigrant wage penalties are partly explained by differences in literacy utilization (25–36% of the explained gap in key countries). Limitations include the absence of explicit survey-weight reporting and the fact that the analysis is not ML predictive modeling.
